How can we implement non‑blocking broadcast to all clients without causing message delays?
What is the safest way to enforce nickname uniqueness across multiple threads or selectors?

claims.text: Threading uses multiple OS threads and works well for I/O‑bound tasks, while asyncio provides task‑level concurrency without extra threads.
Asyncio is part of the standard library since Python 3.4 and offers an alternative to threading for handling many TCP clients.
The GIL restricts threading performance for CPU‑bound work because only one thread can execute Python bytecode at a time.
Scaling a thread pool beyond a few hundred threads can cause a performance drop of 20% or more, showing a saturation cliff.
High thread counts are needed to hide I/O latency on constrained devices, but the GIL serializes execution, limiting CPU usage efficiency.
Sockets return as writable only when outbound network buffer space is available, which can be used to avoid blocking when a client is slow.
The select module can detect when a socket would block, helping implement back‑pressure handling for slow receivers.
Without flushing output buffers, a sender may wait indefinitely because data remains in the buffer and not yet sent to the client.

evidence.quote:
asyncio offers an alternative approach to achieving task level
concurrency without requiring the use of multiple operating system threads

threading is still an appropriate model if you want to run
multiple I/O-bound tasks simultaneously

the GIL limits the performance gains of threading when it comes to
CPU-bound tasks, as only one thread can execute Python bytecode at a time

In CPython, due to the Global Interpreter Lock, only one thread
can execute Python code at once (even though certain performance-oriented
libraries might overcome this limitation)
We demonstrate that naive thread pool scaling causes a "saturation cliff": a performance degradation of >= 20% at overprovisioned thread counts (N >= 512) on edge representative configurations

Deploying Python-based AI agents on resource-constrained edge devices presents a critical runtime optimization challenge: high thread counts are needed to mask I/O latency, yet Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) serializes execution
Advisor "Roofline Analysis" helps to identify if given loop/function is memory or CPU bound
It also identifies under optimized loops that can have a high impact on performance if optimized

concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor offers a higher level interface
to push tasks to a background thread without blocking execution of the
calling thread, while still being able to retrieve their results when needed

Now we come to the major stumbling block of sockets - send and recv operate
on the network buffers

Without a flush in
there, you may wait forever for the reply, because the request may still be in
your output buffer

any reasonably healthy socket will return as writable - it
just means outbound network buffer space is available

select can be handy even with blocking sockets. It’s one way of
determining whether you will block - the socket returns as readable when there’s
something in the buffers
CPython natively supports asyncio since Version 3.4, alternative implementations exist like greenlet, eventlet and gevent, PyPy
Python has support for coroutines using the asyncio.create_task() function

sub_questions.success_criteria: Answer must outline a method (e.g., using send buffers, write‑ready checks, or queue per client) that avoids blocking the server.

sub_questions.success_criteria: Answer must mention using time.monotonic or time.perf_counter around send/receive and calculating round‑trip time.
